We thank the reviewer for a careful and constructive report. We have restructured the work
as a manuscript (code and validation moved to the Supplement and the repository), narrowed it
to Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and the frontotemporal dementia
(FTD) syndromes (Parkinson's disease removed), and framed it as a comparison of network
measures across two spatially distinct cortical neurodegenerative diseases. Every comment
led to new analyses. Below, reviewer text is quoted, followed by our response and the changes.
All numbers are computed from the same cached results as the manuscript.

## Major comment 1 — Spatial interpolation, Euclidean distance and the NDM

> *Euclidean distance is used rather than geodesic cortical distance … Re-running the
> distance baseline and distance-censoring with surface geodesic distance … is essential.*

We computed geodesic distances along the fsaverage5 midthickness surface (medial wall
removed) with the heat method, validated against the analytic geodesic on the sphere (312 vs
314 mm; plain Dijkstra on the same mesh gave 664 mm and was rejected). Contrary to the
concern, **the geodesic kernel predicts atrophy better than the Euclidean kernel**, not worse
(AD r = `r f2(rv("ctx400_geo", 0, "distance", "AD"))` vs `r f2(rv("ctx400_euc", 0, "distance", "AD"))`;
bvFTD `r f2(rv("ctx400_geo", 0, "distance", "bvFTD"))` vs `r f2(rv("ctx400_euc", 0, "distance", "bvFTD"))`;
svPPA `r f2(rv("ctx400_geo", 0, "distance", "svPPA"))` vs `r f2(rv("ctx400_euc", 0, "distance", "svPPA"))`),
and it retains more predictive power when nearby regions are excluded. The spatial
organisation of atrophy therefore follows the cortical sheet; Euclidean distance does not
inflate the baseline by bridging fissures. For censoring we kept Euclidean distance because
volumetric smoothing of DBM maps acts in Euclidean space and Euclidean censoring is the
stricter choice (geodesic ≥ Euclidean within a hemisphere). All structural communication
models still fail to exceed either baseline (Figure 2; Supplementary Tables S6–S7).

> *The network diffusion model is mis-specified … it should be run generatively from
> candidate epicentres and compared against a generative isotropic/geodesic diffusion model
> from the same epicentres.*

We agree and have added exactly this analysis (Methods, "Generative spreading from seeds";
Figure 4). Network diffusion x(t) = e^{−Lt}x₀ on the SC (and on the FC) was seeded at every
node and every bilateral homologue pair, and compared with isotropic Euclidean and geodesic
spread from the same seeds; seed and parameter were refitted in every surrogate. SC
diffusion was never better than spatial spread. In AD, geodesic spread from bilateral anterior
temporal seeds outperformed SC diffusion (r = `r f2(gen("ctx400_geo", "spread_geodesic", "AD")$r)` vs
`r f2(gen("ctx400_geo", "NDM_SC", "AD")$r)`; paired variogram p
`r fp(gdiff("ctx400_geo", "NDM_SC", "spread_geodesic", "AD")$p_variogram)`). We have removed the
statement that "the best diffusion is one step"; we now describe the static heat-kernel
result only as what it is (a smoothing filter applied to an already smooth map) and base our
conclusions about spreading on the generative analysis.

## Major comment 2 — Cortex-only parcellation

We added 14 subcortical structures (Tian S1, mapped to the 14 ENIGMA structures and linked to
the HCP SC and FC provided with Schaefer-400). Because DBM spreads ventricular expansion into
neighbouring tissue, we sampled the core of each structure (≥ 3 mm from template CSF): this
doubled the AD hippocampal value (mean −t 1.6 → 3.0) and left the caudate dominated by
ventricular expansion, which we flag. The 414-node analyses use variogram, Moran and rewiring
nulls (spins rotate the cortex and permute the subcortex).

With the subcortex included, **the structural models still did not survive the variogram
null in AD** (search information r = `r f2(rv("sub414_euc", 0, "search_prob", "AD"))`,
p `r fp(pv("sub414_euc", 0, "search_prob", "AD"))`), and seeded SC diffusion and spatial spread
were indistinguishable; all AD models selected the bilateral amygdala as the seed. Thresholded
FC gained a modest long-range contribution in AD (R = 30 mm: r = `r f2(rv("sub414_euc", 30, "FC_top10", "AD"))`,
variogram p `r fp(pv("sub414_euc", 30, "FC_top10", "AD"))`). We have revised the
interpretation accordingly: our negative conclusion concerns the information in a young-adult
tractography connectome at group level, not axonal spread as such, and we discuss the
under-sampling of temporo-limbic and commissural tracts (Discussion, Limitations).

## Major comment 3 — Negative FC–hub correlation in bvFTD

We used the SPM12 mean EPI template as an open proxy for susceptibility-related signal loss.
As the reviewer anticipated, regional EPI signal is lowest in orbitofrontal and temporal-pole
parcels (limbic network `r f2(res$epi_by_network %>% filter(network == "Limbic") %>% pull(epi_signal))`
of the cortical median) and FC strength tracks it
(ρ = `r f2(res$hubs$ctx400 %>% filter(strength == "FC", syndrome == "AD") %>% pull(rho_strength_epi))`).
Partialling out EPI signal changed the bvFTD association from
ρ = `r f2(res$hubs$ctx400 %>% filter(strength == "FC", syndrome == "bvFTD") %>% pull(rho))` to
`r f2(res$hubs$ctx400 %>% filter(strength == "FC", syndrome == "bvFTD") %>% pull(rho_partial_epi))` (Table 1).
We no longer interpret the association as sparing of functional hubs, and we discuss the
dropout confound. We also added proportional thresholding of FC (strongest 20% and 10% of
edges) throughout: thresholding strengthened the FC–atrophy relationship substantially
(bvFTD, R = 30 mm: full FC r = `r f2(rv("ctx400_euc", 30, "FC", "bvFTD"))`, top 10%
r = `r f2(rv("ctx400_euc", 30, "FC_top10", "bvFTD"))`), and the long-range FC effect in FTD is
now a main result. HCP tSNR maps require ConnectomeDB access; we note this as a limitation.

## Major comment 4 — Template mismatch and DBM-specific smoothing

We registered the FSL MNI152 brain to the ICBM 2009c symmetric brain with ANTs SyN and warped
the Schaefer and Tian atlases with nearest-label interpolation. Registration raised the
template intensity correlation from `r f2(res$registration$intensity_r_before)` to
`r f2(res$registration$intensity_r_after)`; `r round(100 * (1 - res$registration$schaefer400$voxel_agreement_warped_vs_worldNN))`%
of cortical voxels changed parcel at 400 parcels (Supplementary Table S1, Figure S1). Parcel
values correlated r = `r f2(min(res$warp_vs_old$r_warped_vs_worldNN))`–`r f2(max(res$warp_vs_old$r_warped_vs_worldNN))`
with the earlier ones, and all analyses were re-run with the warped atlas. We were not able
to test a surface-based cortical-thickness dataset: the ENIGMA summary statistics do not
include AD or FTD, and we did not substitute other data. We state this in the Limitations,
together with the DBM-specific issues (ventricular spill-over, upstream smoothing).

## Major comment 5 — Null-model asymmetry and negative-r p-values

We now count a test as evidence of a positive network constraint only if r > 0 and FDR
q < 0.05 (Methods, "Null models and inference"; Figure 5). This removes the negative-r
"hits" the reviewer identified (navigation at R = 30 mm in AD and nfvPPA, and diffusion
efficiency throughout). We discuss explicitly that degree-preserving rewiring is
anticonservative (it roughly doubles the mean edge length) and that geometry-preserving
rewiring is conservative (about half of the edges cannot move), and we report how the
geometry-preserving null depends on the bin width (5–40 bins; Supplementary Table S9b).
Our conclusions rest on effects that survive the variogram null, which is independent of
the connectome.

## Major comment 6 — Asymmetric eigenmode bases

We now compute all three bases within each hemisphere: Laplace–Beltrami modes of that
hemisphere's surface and harmonics of that hemisphere's SC and FC graphs, and reconstruct
each hemisphere separately (Table 2, Supplementary Table S13).

## Major comment 7 — Map units and cross-cohort confounds

We have written to the authors of the maps asking for the statistic in the FTD-variant maps,
sample sizes, whether the variant maps share controls, model covariates and smoothing; we
will report their answer. In the meantime the manuscript states that the variant maps may not
be t-statistics and that all analyses are invariant to linear rescaling. Between-syndrome
similarity is now reported only descriptively in the Supplement (Table S5), with the
shared-control caveat. PD has been removed.

## Minor comments

- **Spin variogram ratio discrepancy.** Corrected. The Summary value (≈1.9×) referred to the
  first distance bin only; the manuscript now reports the mean over the five shortest bins
  (`r f2(min(res$null_diag %>% filter(null == "spin") %>% pull(variogram_ratio_bins1to5)))`–`r f2(max(res$null_diag %>% filter(null == "spin") %>% pull(variogram_ratio_bins1to5)))`
  across syndromes) and gives both in Supplementary Table S9.
- **FDR for FC at R = 30 mm.** FC (full and thresholded) is now included in the FDR family
  (Supplementary Table S6).
- **Mirrored-rank logic.** Rewritten as the two-step argument the reviewer proposes
  (Results, "Two distinct atrophy topographies"): the raw left parcel exceeds the raw right
  parcel, but sampling the mirrored map with the same left parcel does not reduce its value,
  so the raw difference reflects parcel geometry, not a hemispheric difference in disease.
- **Formatting and figures.** The work is now an IMRaD manuscript with a separate Supplement;
  code, package notes and validation logs are in the repository. Figures were redrawn: the
  scatter grid was removed, parcel lists are no longer clipped, and figures are sized to fit
  a page.
